classification.reason: The coach analyzes pro match footage to explain the concept of fault tolerance, but does not provide any actionable drill, cue, self-check, or exercise for the viewer to execute.

problem.title_as_question: What is fault tolerance in action and why is it essential?
problem.definition: The ability to produce an effective, high-quality shot and stay in the point when out of position or jammed, rather than missing outright.
prerequisites: Rallying against high pace and depth

symptoms.description: The player is forced into an awkward swing up above the head with restricted rotation.
The player shanks the ball into the stands or hits it into the bottom of the net when jammed.
The player floats a passive ball back to the middle and resets to neutral instead of attacking.

causes.statement: The player probes imperfectly with footwork and gets way too close to the ball.
The player's arm cannot properly extend and the hips are stuck due to crowded spacing.
High-level opponent quality and deep incoming shots force the player to hit from an out-of-position state.

angles.summary: The coach reviews pro footage of Cameron Norrie and his opponent exchanging fast inside-in forehands to demonstrate playing under compromised conditions.
Even with compromised footwork and jammed hips, preserving fundamental contact out in front produces an effective shot.
The coach contrasts the jammed forehand with a subsequent shot featuring perfect probing and extension to highlight shot differences.
Winning tennis matches is driven by keeping compromised shots 80% effective rather than focusing solely on producing perfect 100% shots.
